cues: Choosing a degree often starts with choosing a subject. Economics, perhaps. Or politics.
But what if your interests cross those boundaries?
You might want to explore before you specialise, or bring different fields into conversation throughout your studies.
At University College Roosevelt, students can choose courses across six academic clusters. Together, those clusters form the Liberal Arts and Sciences curriculum.
Consider a student interested in economics, politics, and why some countries become rich while others stay poor.
Where could that question take them?

heading: Who benefits from growth?
cues: BENECON111
BENECON212
Start with an open course, Introduction to Economics. How do prices change what households buy, or what firms produce?
BENECON211
At the scale of a country, trade and economic growth come into view.
BENECON311
BENECON314
Taxes change who benefits from growth. Experiments help explain how people respond to those incentives.

heading: How do firms create wealth?
cues: BENGATE101
BENBUSI112
Consider a new business. Can its founders turn an idea into a venture? What do its accounts tell them?
BENBUSI312
BENENTR312
Banks help finance investment. When a firm expands abroad, it faces a different set of rules.
BENBUSI211
And if artificial intelligence raises productivity, who shares in the gains?

heading: What would count as evidence?
cues: BENGATE102
Research methods help the student decide what to measure. Here, Research Methods and Statistics is the gateway course.
BENECON312
Econometrics requires that gateway. Completing it unlocks Econometrics.
Econometrics asks whether investment actually causes growth, or simply moves alongside it.
Markets operate under rules. Who makes those rules? Who benefits from them? That takes us from economics into politics.
heading: Who sets the rules for markets?
Who makes the rules?
cues: GOSPOLI111
GOSPOLI112
Political philosophy asks what makes a distribution fair. Comparative politics examines how different institutions make those choices.
GOSPOLI212
GOSPOLI311
Across borders, states negotiate. The European Union shows how governments make rules together.
GOSGATE102
GOSPOLI313
Law examines how rules work in society. Peace and conflict studies asks how disputes escalate and how reconciliation becomes possible.

heading: How did countries get here?
cues: GOSHIST111
GOSHIST211
Why did countries follow different paths? Industrialisation transformed work. Empires shaped control over land and trade.
GOSHIST312
GOSSOCI212
The student can read historical sources and use qualitative research to understand how these changes shaped people’s lives.

heading: Who decides what lasts?
cues: Questions of power also lead from politics to the environment.

heading: Who shapes environmental policy?
cues: ENSDELT312
When governments, firms and citizens disagree about environmental policy, whose priorities prevail? The governance of sustainability examines how those decisions are made.

heading: How can the student make the case?
cues: ACCPPDE101
Alongside these courses, the student practises writing, presenting an argument and reflecting on what they have learned.
One question about prosperity brought economics into conversation with politics. It also made room for history and sustainability. Together, they form one six-semester programme.
